Local governments have limited power over federal enforcement but they do control their own employees, budgets, and policies.

It's also a direct rebuke of the 287(g) expansion underway nationally. Since January 2025, the number of 287(g) agreements has grown from 134 to over 1,500. Pittsburgh is moving in the opposite direction, and doing so formally, at exactly the moment federal pressure is highest.

The implications are real and immediate. Residents who are undocumented (or who live with someone who is) may now be more willing to call 911, access emergency rooms, send children to school, or utilize city services without fear that contact with city employees triggers ICE.

Two additional bills (which would bar ICE from using city-owned property and require a warrant to enter private city-managed spaces) were held for further legal review. They go further than anything Allegheny County recently passed and will face more scrutiny before a vote.

The second bill passed Tuesday requires the city's Department of Innovation and Performance to audit all surveillance technologies currently in operation. In a moment of rapidly expanding federal surveillance capacity, knowing what tools exist locally is not a small thing.

The law also creates an enforcement mechanism. If a police officer violates the non-cooperation policy, the Citizen Police Review Board investigates. If it's a city employee, the Office of Municipal Investigations handles it. Accountability is now built into the structure.

That matters because promises aren't policy. Former Mayor Ed Gainey, current Mayor Corey O'Connor, and Police Chief Jason Lando had all pledged non-cooperation with ICE. But pledges can be reversed. A codified ordinance cannot be undone without a formal legislative vote.

The first bill makes it illegal under city law for Pittsburgh to sign a 287(g) agreement with ICE. These agreements allow local police to perform federal immigration enforcement duties. Pittsburgh just put that option permanently off the table. In writing, with consequences.

Pittsburgh's City Council voted unanimously this week to formally codify its refusal to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. This is bigger than a symbolic gesture, here's what it actually does and why it matters. 🧵

ICE detention has become a horror movie on par with The Ring: we don't know exactly who will die next, but someone will die every six days. That's what systemic violence looks like when you put numbers to it.

This is what social scientists mean by systemic violence: not a single bad actor, but emergent patterns of harm in systems built on marginalization and neglect. Ninety days and fifteen deaths is a rate that makes that pattern visible in an unusually direct way.

ICE press releases on detained deaths consistently frame them as the fault of the deceased, but a rate of one death every six days points to something structural rather than a series of individual failures or medical anomalies.

ICE detention has become a horror movie on par with The Ring: we don't know exactly who will die next, but someone will die every six days. That's what systemic violence looks like when you put numbers to it.

This is what social scientists mean by systemic violence: not a single bad actor, but emergent patterns of harm in systems built on marginalization and neglect. Ninety days and fifteen deaths is a rate that makes that pattern visible in an unusually direct way.

ICE press releases on detained deaths consistently frame them as the fault of the deceased, but a rate of one death every six days points to something structural rather than a series of individual failures or medical anomalies.

Miami Correctional only started holding ICE detainees in October 2025. Indiana earns $291/day per detainee, nearly 4x what it pays for state inmates. A congressional visit found delayed medical care, lost belongings, and barriers to legal access.
Tuan Van Bui came to the U.S. in 1990 on an AM-1 visa under the little discussed (these days) Amerasian Homecoming Act, created for Vietnamese children fathered by U.S. soldiers.
ICE has reported the 15th death in immigration detention in 2026. Tuan Van Bui, 55, died April 1 at Miami Correctional Center in Indiana. That's one death every 6.0 days since January 1. 🧵
